strengths: The paper addresses an underexplored problem (image-to-brain signal encoding with real brain responses as supervision), which is a reasonable and interesting direction complementary to the well-studied brain decoding literature.
Unlike the closest prior work (Img2EEG, Lu & Golomb 2024), the model generates brain signals at the full original dimensionality (63x250 EEG; 271x200 MEG), which is a meaningful improvement in scope.

Experiments are conducted on two public multimodal datasets (THINGS-EEG2 and THINGS-MEG), with both within-subject and cross-subject evaluations, an ablation of conditioning strategies (addition vs. concatenation vs. cross-attention), and extensive topography visualizations for all subjects.
The limitations discussion is reasonably honest, acknowledging computational constraints and the difficulty of cross-subject variability.
weaknesses: The central claim of generating 'biologically plausible' brain signals is not convincingly supported by the evidence. Within-subject PCC is only 0.188 (EEG) and 0.122 (MEG), and the generated MEG topographies in Figures 4 and 8 are visibly much weaker in amplitude and spatially different from real MEG signals, which appears to contradict the paper's claims rather than support them.

There is no comparison against any external baseline (e.g., Img2EEG, simple regression/encoder-decoder models), and critically, no trivial baseline such as predicting the mean training evoked response. Given such low PCC values, it is unclear whether the diffusion model outperforms a constant or average-signal predictor, which undermines the significance of the reported numbers.

The motivation for using a diffusion model is not justified. Image-to-brain mapping conditioned on the image is essentially a conditional regression problem; a diffusion sampler introduces stochasticity, yet the paper neither analyzes how sampling noise affects MSE/PCC nor compares against a deterministic regression baseline. The standard DDPM machinery (Eqs. 5-14) and cross-attention conditioning (Eqs. 7-10) are directly borrowed from prior work (Ho et al. 2020; Stable Diffusion-style UNet2DConditionModel), so the methodological novelty is thin.

The connection to visual prostheses is asserted but never substantiated. Actual prosthesis encoding requires predicting electrical stimulation patterns that produce useful phosphenes, not scalp EEG/MEG recordings; no phosphene model, decoding pipeline, or downstream task is used to validate that the generated signals are useful for the stated application. The framing feels like a wrapper around a signal-generation experiment.

Ablation improvements are small (e.g., MSE 0.217 vs. 0.228 for concatenation on EEG; PCC 0.188 vs. 0.180) with no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds, so the claim that cross-attention provides a consistent advantage is weakly evidenced. On MEG, cross-attention PCC (0.122) actually trails addition in several subjects.

Cross-subject results are very poor (PCC ~0.05-0.10 on both datasets), which the authors attribute to inter-subject variability, but no mitigation (e.g., subject embedding, normalization) is attempted or discussed as future work, limiting the practical reach of the contribution.

Presentation issues reduce clarity: first-person statements ('I have plotted the topography...'), confusing table layouts (Table 1 places the 'Average' column before subject columns), inconsistent metric reporting, and no mention of code release, weakening reproducibility.

The supervised-signal argument against prior work (Granley et al.; Wang et al.) is somewhat overstated: using paired image-brain datasets as supervision is a straightforward consequence of dataset choice, not a methodological contribution in itself.

strengths: Targets an under-explored problem: supervised image-to-brain encoding using paired image–M/EEG datasets (THINGS-EEG2, THINGS-MEG), in contrast to prior visual prosthesis encoding work that lacks real brain responses as supervision.
Evaluates on two large public multimodal datasets and reports both within-subject and cross-subject results, with an ablation comparing cross-attention, concatenation, and addition conditioning.

The topography visualizations (training vs. test vs. generated M/EEG) are a thoughtful qualitative addition, and the honest discussion of train/test distribution differences and inter-subject variability is a positive.
The method maintains the full original output dimensionality of the recordings (63×250 EEG, 271×200 MEG), which the authors argue is an improvement over Img2EEG's reduced representation.
weaknesses: No baseline comparisons. The central claim of 'high-quality conversion from images to brain signals' is unsupported because the paper never compares against any alternative: neither the closest prior work (Img2EEG, Lu & Golomb 2024), nor simple deterministic regressors (e.g., ridge regression or a CLIP-to-signal MLP), nor even the ablation variants as a head-to-head in the main text. Without baselines, the absolute numbers (PCC ≈ 0.19 EEG, 0.12 MEG) cannot be interpreted as good or bad.

The methodological choice of a diffusion model is not justified. For conditional generation evaluated by MSE/PCC against ground truth, a stochastic generative model is at an inherent disadvantage to a deterministic regressor; the paper offers no evidence that iterative denoising is preferable here, making the DDPM framing appear unmotivated rather than a deliberate design choice.

The evaluation protocol is under-specified and possibly invalid. Test data contain many repetitions (80 for EEG), yet it is unclear whether the generated signal is compared against averaged test responses or single trials; single-trial M/EEG has very low SNR, and the discrepancy would dramatically change interpretation of the PCC values. Details such as the variance schedule T, number of sampling steps, and how MSE/PCC are computed per subject are missing.

The key ablation shows only marginal gains for cross-attention (EEG MSE 0.217 vs 0.227/0.228; EEG PCC 0.188 vs 0.180/0.172; MEG PCC 0.122 vs 0.118 for addition), with no statistical significance testing, no multiple seeds, and per-subject results that are inconsistent (e.g., cross-attention loses to addition/concatenation on several subjects). The claim that cross-attention enables 'fine-grained alignment' is weakly supported.

The visual prosthesis motivation is largely disconnected from what is actually done. The paper motivates generating biologically plausible *stimuli* for electrode arrays, but the method generates scalp M/EEG recordings, not prosthesis stimuli, and no downstream task (e.g., decoding, phosphene simulation, stimulus recovery) demonstrates that the generated signals are 'biologically plausible' beyond raw correlation. The claimed contribution to visual prostheses is therefore overstated.

The cross-subject generalization claims are internally inconsistent. The text claims 'good cross-subject generalization capability' based on small standard deviations in Table 2, yet cross-subject PCC (Table 9: ~0.10) drops to roughly half of within-subject PCC (~0.19), and the authors themselves later acknowledge substantial degradation. The framing cherry-picks favorable statistics.

The novelty is limited: the method is essentially a standard HuggingFace UNet2DConditionModel with CLIP conditioning applied to M/EEG signals — a configuration swap rather than a new technique, and the cross-attention mechanism is textbook (Vaswani et al.). The conceptual contribution does not meet the bar of a main-track ICML paper.

Presentation problems undermine credibility: Table 1's header is malformed (column labels misaligned with values); Section 4.4 begins with the odd first-person 'I have plotted'; the terminology in Figure 1 (labeling the phosphene model stage 'brain decoding') contradicts the definitions given in the same paragraph; and notation in Eqs. (2)–(4) is imprecise (decoder shown taking h_img and t redundantly).

Reproducibility is inadequate: no code release, no full hyperparameter specification (T, β schedule, sampling steps), and no statement on statistical testing. The limitation discussion acknowledges only compute constraints on model depth, ignoring the more fundamental evaluation weaknesses.

strengths: The paper targets the relatively underexplored brain encoding (image-to-brain) direction, in contrast to the heavily studied brain decoding literature, which is a reasonable and potentially useful problem framing.

The use of paired multimodal datasets (THINGS-EEG2 and THINGS-MEG) to provide real brain responses as supervision directly addresses a recognized weakness in prior prosthesis stimulus-encoding work (e.g., Granley et al.), and the framework is evaluated on both EEG and MEG.

The evaluation includes within-subject, cross-subject, and ablation (addition vs. concatenation vs. cross-attention) experiments, plus extensive topography visualizations that give qualitative insight into train/test/generated signal differences and inter-subject variability.
The limitations are discussed honestly (e.g., computational constraints preventing deeper architectures), and the discussion of why generated topographies diverge from test topographies is candid.
weaknesses: No baselines are compared against. There is no linear regression, MLP, Img2EEG, or even a trivial 'predict the dataset-average evoked response' baseline. Given that the reported PCC is only ~0.188 (EEG) and ~0.122 (MEG), it is entirely possible the model mostly reproduces the generic, image-independent evoked response rather than image-specific brain activity. Without baselines, the central claim that the framework achieves 'high-quality' image-to-brain conversion is unsupported.

The central claim of 'biological plausibility' is not validated in any meaningful downstream sense. The paper criticizes prior work for lacking validation against real brain responses, but MSE/PCC against averaged signals is a weak proxy: it does not demonstrate that generated signals carry image-specific information (e.g., no retrieval accuracy, classification from generated signals, or decoding the generated signals back to images). The paper's own motivation demands a stronger evaluation than it delivers.

The technical novelty is limited. A DDPM with cross-attention conditioning on CLIP embeddings is essentially the standard conditional diffusion recipe (e.g., UNet2DConditionModel from HuggingFace diffusers with CrossAttn blocks is used almost out of the box). The ablation gains are small (e.g., MSE 0.217 vs. 0.228 for concatenation; PCC 0.188 vs. 0.180) and no statistical significance tests, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed variance are reported, so the claimed advantage of cross-attention is not statistically established.

The connection to visual prostheses is overclaimed and underdeveloped. The framework generates EEG/MEG signals from images, but a retinal prosthesis requires predicting stimulation patterns, not sensor-space recordings. The paper never closes the loop with a phosphene model, downstream decoding, or any prosthesis-relevant evaluation, so the prosthesis framing in the title and abstract is largely rhetorical.

Terminology is confusing and nonstandard: the paper calls stimulus prediction 'brain encoding' and phosphene-evoked perception 'brain decoding,' reversing the conventions of the brain decoding literature it cites (Benchetrit et al.). Figure 2 also shows an 'L_MSE' between reconstructed and ground-truth brain signals while Section 3.4 states training uses the noise-prediction objective, creating ambiguity about what is actually optimized.

Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, key hyperparameters (variance schedule, number of diffusion steps T, EMA, sampling details) are unspecified, and preprocessing is only referenced via another paper (Song et al., 2025).

Presentation issues: first-person singular appears in Section 4.4 ('I have plotted the topography'), Table 1's column layout is confusingly ordered (the 'Average' column precedes subjects 1-10), and several result claims (e.g., cross-subject generalization being 'good' based on tiny standard deviations) are inconsistent with the very low cross-subject PCC values (~0.05-0.10 in Tables 9-10), which actually indicate poor generalization.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: image-to-brain (M/EEG) signal generation (brain encoding) using real paired image-brain data, in contrast to prior visual-prosthesis encoding work that used synthetic stimuli (MNIST/COCO) without real neural supervision (Granley et al.; Wang et al.).

The framework is cleanly described: DiT + DDIM backbone, cross-attention conditioning on concatenated CLIP image and LLM-caption text embeddings, and learnable spatio-temporal (brain-region + temporal) position embeddings. The problem formulation, training/inference algorithms (Appendix C), preprocessing, and architecture details (Appendices D-E) support reproducibility.

Reasonably comprehensive experiments: within-subject and cross-subject settings on two datasets (THINGS-EEG2, THINGS-MEG), component ablations (Tables 3-4), LLM-caption comparisons with CLIP Score distributions (Tables 5-8), and brain-region ablations whose occipital-cortex finding is consistent with neuroscience knowledge.

Honest treatment of limitations: the paper transparently reports the substantial cross-subject performance degradation and analyzes it via topography difference figures (Figures 3 and 7), rather than hiding a negative result. Includes an impact statement.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the contribution is largely a recombination of established components (DiT, DDIM, CLIP conditioning, cross-attention, learnable positional embeddings) applied to a new modality. This is acceptable as application-driven work, but the paper's framing as a 'novel framework' overstates the technical advance.

Evaluation methodology for a generative model is under-specified and potentially questionable: it is unclear whether the MSE/Pearson/cosine metrics compare a single stochastic DDIM sample against one ground-truth trial, an averaged trial, or multiple samples. Since the diffusion model is stochastic and EEG/MEG test trials are noisy, point-comparison metrics may not fairly measure generation quality, and the paper does not clarify or justify this protocol.

No statistical significance testing, variance, or per-subject results are reported; all tables give only means averaged across 10 (EEG) or 4 (MEG) subjects, making it hard to judge reliability of the improvements over SynBrain.

The baseline set is weak: the main comparisons are 2014/2015 CNN-feature linear regression encoding models and SynBrain, which was designed for fMRI and had to be adapted for M/EEG. No recent strong generative baselines or even a simpler conditional diffusion/regression variant conditioned only on CLIP image embeddings (beyond the ablation removing text) are provided.

The link to the visual-prosthesis pipeline is largely motivational: the method generates brain signals from images, whereas a prosthesis ultimately requires stimulus prediction. The paper does not demonstrate any downstream use (e.g., closed-loop evaluation or comparison of generated signals to evoked responses), so the practical significance for prostheses remains aspirational.

Internal inconsistencies raise concerns about care: Figure 2/Section 3.2.3 state ViT-L/14 produces 257 tokens of dimension 768, but CLIP ViT-L/14 has a 1024-dimensional output (768 corresponds to ViT-B); the EEG patch count '16 x 63 = 1008' conflates patch grid ordering and padding is not fully explained.
No code release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility of the reported numbers despite the good procedural detail.

No qualitative comparison of within-subject generated vs. real brain signals (e.g., waveform or topography reconstructions) is shown; the 'biologically plausible' claim rests mostly on aggregate metrics and the SL measure, whose interpretation for a single generated series is not carefully justified.

strengths: Addresses an under-explored problem: image-to-brain-signal generation (encoding) for M/EEG using datasets with paired image and brain data, in contrast to prior visual prosthesis encoding work that lacks real neural supervision (e.g., Granley et al., 2022/2023; Wang et al.).

The framework is clearly described, with pseudocode for training and inference, dataset preprocessing details, metric definitions, and architecture hyperparameters that collectively support reasonable reproducibility.

Experiments cover both THINGS-EEG2 and THINGS-MEG, include a cross-subject setting, and are accompanied by ablations of the main components (CLIP text conditioning, region and temporal embeddings) and an LLM comparison.
The brain-region ablation analysis (occipital channels matter most) is a nice sanity check that connects model behavior to established neuroscience knowledge about visual processing.
The paper is honest that cross-subject generalization remains a major open challenge and does not overclaim success there.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is essentially a direct application of DiT + cross-attention conditioning on CLIP embeddings, plus standard additive learnable position embeddings. Each component is well-established, and the paper does not identify or solve a fundamentally new technical challenge.

The central claim of generating 'biologically plausible' brain signals is not adequately supported. MSE, Pearson, cosine, and SL against ground-truth signals measure reconstruction fidelity, not biological plausibility; there is no downstream evaluation (e.g., decoding generated signals back to images, comparison of evoked-response timing profiles, expert evaluation) that would substantiate this claim.

Baselines are weak and poorly matched: Güçlü & Van Gerven (2015) and Yamins et al. (2014) are decade-old fMRI-ventral-stream methods, apparently re-implemented for M/EEG, and SynBrain was designed for fMRI and only 'adapted' by the authors. No modern EEG/MEG generative baselines (e.g., EEG GAN/diffusion augmentation methods cited in the related work) or conditional regression baselines are compared, making the headline improvements hard to interpret.

No statistical rigor: results are averaged over subjects with no variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests, despite known large inter-subject variability (which the paper itself demonstrates in Figure 3). Several ablation gains (e.g., w/o CLIP text: 0.425 vs 0.405 Pearson) may not be meaningful.

Cross-subject results are very poor (Pearson 0.157 EEG, 0.082 MEG) and are only computed with a single training subject, yet Figure 3's subject-to-subject topography difference is presented as an explanation when it is a near-tautological observation.

The connection to visual prostheses is stretched: the framework generates sensor-level M/EEG signals, not stimulation parameters or cortical responses, and no experiment demonstrates any benefit to an actual prosthetic pipeline (encoding-to-phosphene closed loop).

There is a technical inconsistency: the paper states CLIP ViT-L/14 produces embeddings of dimension D=768, but ViT-L has a hidden dimension of 1024 (768 is ViT-B), raising questions about implementation details.

The caption-quality analysis is circular: CLIP Score evaluates captions with the same CLIP model family used for conditioning, so high scores do not independently validate that captions improve brain-signal generation; the ablation showing only a modest gain from text conditioning further weakens this motivation.
No limitations section, no mention of code release, and no discussion of ethical considerations around medical/prosthetic claims beyond a brief impact statement.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely under-explored problem: image-to-brain-signal generation (brain encoding) for M/EEG, which is far less developed than brain decoding, and situates it within a plausible visual-prosthesis pipeline.

The technical framework is reasonable and clearly described: DiT with DDIM, cross-attention with brain-signal embeddings as Query and concatenated CLIP image + LLM-generated caption text embeddings as Key/Value, plus a learnable spatio-temporal position encoding (region + temporal embeddings) that is sensibly motivated by M/EEG structure.

Evaluation spans two standard multimodal benchmarks (THINGS-EEG2, THINGS-MEG) with both within-subject and cross-subject settings, and the paper includes ablations for each proposed component (CLIP text embeddings, region embeddings, temporal embeddings) and an LLM-choice comparison.
The brain-region ablation study (Figure 6) is a nice touch: the finding that removing occipital channels hurts most is consistent with visual neuroscience and adds a degree of interpretability.
Appendices provide training/inference pseudocode, preprocessing details, region-to-channel mappings, and metric definitions, which support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central claim that the method generates 'biologically plausible' brain signals is not adequately supported. All evaluation is generic signal-similarity (MSE, Pearson, cosine, SL) between generated and ground-truth signals. There is no downstream validation (e.g., decoding generated signals back to stimulus category, retrieval accuracy against held-out images), no analysis of evoked components (e.g., N170/P300 timing), and no comparison of generated vs. real topography statistics. 'Biological plausibility' is asserted, not demonstrated.

Baseline comparison is weak. The two main baselines are 2014/2015 regression encoding models (Guçlü & Van Gerven; Yamins et al.) that were never designed for generative M/EEG synthesis, plus SynBrain, which was designed for fMRI and only adapted by the authors. No comparison to existing EEG/MEG generation approaches (e.g., GAN-based EEG synthesis such as EEG-GAN variants) or to strong modern regression encoders makes the claimed superiority hard to interpret.

No statistical rigor: results are single numbers with no variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests, even though within-subject results are averaged over 10 EEG subjects and the gap to the best baseline (e.g., MSE 0.109 vs 0.156) is not tested. Diffusion models are stochastic; it is also unclear how generated samples are matched to ground truth (single sample? trial-averaged?) — a methodological detail that materially affects all reported metrics.

The motivation-to-method link is loose. The paper motivates visual prostheses, which require predicting stimulation patterns, but the framework generates M/EEG recordings, not stimuli. The pipeline in Figure 1 (image sensor → processing → stimulus → phosphene model) is never actually instantiated; generated M/EEG is not shown to improve any prosthesis-stage quantity. The prosthesis framing overstates the practical significance of the contribution.

Cross-subject generalization is essentially unresolved: performance collapses (Pearson 0.425→0.157 on EEG, 0.379→0.082 on MEG), yet the paper offers only a descriptive topography comparison rather than attempting or discussing standard mitigation (subject-wise normalization, per-subject adapters, alignment losses), limiting the work's usefulness for realistic BCIs.

Ablation effects for the headline component are small: removing CLIP text embeddings changes MSE only from 0.117 to 0.109 (EEG) and 0.677 to 0.663 (MEG), without variance estimates; whether the LLM-caption machinery (a significant part of the framing) is worth its complexity is not established. The caption-quality analysis (CLIP Score distributions) is also somewhat circular — it shows the captions are well aligned to images, not that they help generate brain signals.

Technical inconsistencies undermine confidence: the paper states CLIP ViT-L/14 produces 768-dimensional embeddings, but ViT-L/14 has a 1024-dimensional hidden size; the patch/region partitioning details (e.g., padding for 63 channels with 4×4 patches, MEG 68×50=3400 patches) are described only loosely. No code release is mentioned.

Writing in places over-claims and under-hedges: 'consistently outperforms all baseline methods' rests on three baselines, and the contribution list presents standard components (DiT, cross-attention, LLM captions, positional embeddings) as the primary novelty rather than carefully articulating what is new relative to prior encoding work.
